All of this underlines Dr. Bernanke’s congressional testimony at the end of February, to the effect that the healthy national US growth rate in the fourth quarter of 2009 (fourth GDP was up by an annualised 5.9%) was based on inventory rebuilding.  Such growth is by definition temporary and the problems outlined above, including the budget deficit, have led Dr. Bernanke to assert that the federal funds rate needs to be held down for an extended period. 

As discussed in the gold chapter of this publication, the implications behind this point to renewed gold investment demand.  Loss of confidence in economic growth - and economic policies - is expected to rekindle investor demand for gold as this year wears on, especially if a double-dip 

recession develops.  Few fiat currencies are likely to find investor favour especially when the dollar succumbs to the economic forces that will develop as a result of the massive quantitative easing programmes that have been put in place. This includes the prospect of accelerating inflationary forces, boosted by artificially low interest rates, and the arguments for fresh gold investment are clear. 

###### **Sovereign debt problems remain a key issue, with political ramifications** 

In the short term, however, the dollar looks likely to strengthen (before weakening again later in the year).  The Greek government has produced its third austerity package in as many months, but the recovery process is not yet in train, there is domestic upheaval within the country, including widespread strike action and there is still the possibility that the country may have to resort to the IMF.

The weakness of the euro in its own right, combined with independent international strength in the dollar, meant that while the net change in the gold price in dollar terms over the month was a 3% gain, in euro terms gold rose by 5% to register a new record high at the start of March. Essentially the dollar price continued to consolidate during February in an effort to reverse a short term down trend, but (as is also the case with silver) the medium-term uptrend remained intact, with a degree of technical support now offered on the charts. As a result, with the dollar easing in early March, the dollar price is aiming for six-week highs towards $1,150. Market sentiment is improving, but there is still a degree of caution for the short term; the longer term outlook remains more constructive. New peaks have also been reached in sterling terms as the UK currency has slid heavily, while the Swiss franc denominated price gained 5% during February. Gold remains some 12% off its January 1980 record in Swiss franc terms, and is 52% off the yen record, set on the same date. Selling was largely professional and dollar-related and, when the dollar started to ease at the start of the sec

ond week of February, selling pressure abated and gold actually rallied quite sharply, bouncing up from $1,045 towards $1,075 in the space of one day. Market sentiment was given a boost, as prices were turning, by reports that China’s sovereign wealth fund had taken a stake (equivalent to 4.5 tonnes) in the SPDR® Gold Shares fund during the fourth quarter of 2009. Later in the month there was a degree of confusion about the proposals for IMF gold sales, with a spate of rumours that the remaining metal, which the Fund has said may be sold into the market (in part if not in total) will in fact be sold elsewhere in the official sector, with India and China being cited as likely counterparties. There has been little to substantiate these rumours, however and it would still appear at the start of March that some if not all of this IMF gold (which amounts to 191.3 tonnes) will be sold into the free market - very probably under the auspices of the third Central Bank Gold Agreement. At the start of March the market has been benefiting from the return of fund-led investment buying. ###### **Recent PGM market developments; platinum jewellery strong for much of February, but this may be partly for seasonal reasons** The key to the platinum jewellery market is, of course, China, in which platinum jewellery demand peaked in 2002, when it reached 1.67 million ounces, or 22% of global fabrication demand. This dropped to less than a million ounces in 2008, but staged a substantial recovery last year, largely in response to the drop in price, and may have reached as much as 1.5 million ounces. The accelerated rally in platinum prices in the final weeks of last year and its sustained strength in the early weeks of this year have been undermining local Chinese jewellery demand, although interest was lively in advance of the Chinese New Year celebrations in the middle of February, and appeared to be running roughly in line with early 2009. Figures since then have suggested that demand following the New Year celebrations has been sluggish, but this is not unusual. Platinum’s premium over both gold and palladium has been increasing steadily, however, (see charts on following pages) and this may yet put the platinum jewellery sector under renewed pressure, especially given that the increase has been because all the metals have been enjoying bull markets, rather than the opposite scenario, with prices falling and gold falling faster than platinum. The market will be watching the Chinese government’s next statements closely in order to assess the outlook for the renminbi as any strengthening obviously works in favour of the consumer and once again the subject is a popular topic for debate - even though the effective exchange rate has barely moved in recent months. The use of monetary policy and bank reserve requirements to achieve a soft landing, rather than hiking interest rates, suggests that any appreciation in the renminbi is likely to be gradual, especially as recent Chinese inflation figures have been more benign than expected; January CPI was up by just 1.5% year-onyear, although the PPI was up by 4.3%. The annual meeting of the National People’s Congress takes place at the end of the first week of March and is expected to focus on widening domestic consumption and reducing the economy’s reliance on exports.
